name: Book discussion | 'A Sort of Homecoming': Indian fiction writing in 2026
description: What’s Indian fiction writing in 2026 like? Between evolving readership, self-publishing platforms, AI writing and translations, how has an author’s journey changed? Join us for a retrospective with  The Deodar Prize  authors as they talk about their experiences and unveil the best stories of 2026, with  Aadit Basu , the 2026 winner and  Sumanya Velamur , shortlisted in 2024 in conversation with  Ratul Ghosh , the runner-up for The Deodar Prize in 2023. This will be followed by an interactive Q&A with the audience. Here are the details: Date:   21 November 2026, Saturday Time:  6:00 PM  Venue:  Champaca Bookstore, Vasanthnagar RSVP here to register. About the book: Tigers can be pets. The government can snatch your home. A midlife crisis can land you, fully clothed, in a swimming pool. From a vengeful goddess to a vomiting rice cooker, these stories carefully tread the ordinary alongside the fantastic. Short stories, like dreams, are visceral, vivid and hard to reconstruct; yet each bite leaves a distinct flavour on the tongue. Sweet. Sour. Salty. Spicy. Umami. Pick your flavour. About the speakers:  Sumanya Anand Velamur   is a researcher, social worker, impact consultant, and writer. She is based in Bengaluru. Her fiction and non-fiction works have been published in  Kitaab, Feminism in India, Mean Pepper Vine, USAWA, Out of Print Blog, Quibble Lit,  and  Quillmark . Her stories were longlisted for the Hope Prize, 2025 and shortlisted for the Deodar Prize (and featured in the Deodar 2024 anthology), 2024 and the BWW R.K.Anand Prize, 2024.  Aadit Basu   is a writer and designer based in Bangalore. By day, he is the founder of morphous Design Lab, a studio working at the intersection of craft and technology, solving problems that no one knew they had. He started his career as an architectural photographer, then became an artist investigating contemporary culture, but writing has always been at the heart of it all. He writes across fiction, poetry and cultural criticism, often drawn to memory, the internet and the strange absurdities of urban life. About the moderator: Till he had to care for his father,  Ratul Ghosh   was a conventional engineer-MBA-CXO. As part of the reset, he started writing fiction about suffering and caring. He was runners-up at the inaugural Deodar Prize and was awarded the BWW RK Anand Memorial Award last year. His publications include  Hammock, Usawa, Bangalore Review, Out of Print, Muse India  and  Hooghly Review . He lives in Bangalore and is currently writing a memoir and a collection of short fiction. name: Book Launch | ‘Mahua Matters’: Stories, Memory and Flavour
description: Mahua is more than a flower. Rooted in forest ecologies, community knowledge, food cultures and livelihoods, it carries stories that are often overlooked.  Mahua Matters , a publication by Wild Harvest India and Edible Issues and  Issue 1  brings together these stories through research, writing and flavour exploration.  Join us for a conversation with editors and the  Mahua Matters  team,  Shivani Unakar  and  Elizabeth Yorke , contributor  Kumud Dadlani , and chef  Hanna Sarangan  on the people and places behind the book, followed by a guided tasting that explores mahua’s many flavours and possibilities. Together, we’ll discover what it means to look at this flower in new ways and why its stories matter. This will be followed by an interactive Q&A with the audience. Here are the details: Date:   22 November 2026, Sunday Time:   6:00 PM  Venue:   Champaca Bookstore, Vasanthnagar RSVP here to register. About the book: Mahua Matters   is a collaborative storytelling and engagement project by Wild Harvest and Edible Issues, dedicated to reintroducing and reimagining Mahua – a culturally significant, climate-resilient tree native to central and eastern India. For generations, Mahua flowers, seeds, and oil have been integral to the food, livelihoods, and traditions of many Adivasi and forest-dwelling communities. Yet, outside these communities, Mahua is often misunderstood, reduced to its association with country liquor, and overlooked for its rich cultural, ecological, and culinary value. Mahua Matters ,  Issue #1  brings together essays, research, speculative fiction, and recipes. From forest ecologies and Indigenous foodways, to history and policy, markets and contemporary kitchens, this book acts as a tangible starting point to exploring the multiplicity of mahua in India. This issue includes a new moveable Mahua Flavour Wheel—developed over a year of participatory Mahua Flavour Labs and public tastings—for readers to explore this ingredient in their own kitchens. About the speakers:  Elizabeth Yorke   is a food systems strategist, entrepreneur and researcher working at the intersection of food, sustainability, culture and innovation. A chef by training, her work explores how food can be a lens for understanding ecological, social and economic change. She is the co-creator of Edible Issues and founder of Saving Grains, and works across research, creative programmes, ventures and collaborations to imagine more resilient and regenerative food futures. Hanna Sarangan   is a Goa-based chef, business owner, and food consultant. With over a decade working in different parts of the world, her passion lies in creating ingredient-driven menus that celebrate foraged local and seasonal ingredients. For the last year, she's been working with Wild Harvest to develop mahua-based recipes, and familiarize consumers with creative ways to bring mahua into their kitchens. Kumud Dadlani   is a food culture strategist and storyteller who believes that eating is a political act. Her work wanders through farms, kitchens, and dining tables, exploring indigenous ingredients, ethical sourcing, and the power of food traditions. A graduate of the University of Gastronomic Sciences in Italy, she has worked with Slow Food International, Diaspora Co., and Impresario Hospitality, and her writing has appeared in Condé Nast Traveller India, The Hindu, and beyond. About the moderator: Shivani Unakar  is a Bangalore-based food culture researcher, exploring the intersection of food, people, and place. Through immersive fieldwork and public engagement, she translates complex food narratives into strategic storytelling and cultural programming for institutions, brands, and community projects.
